job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Sara Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I check ad dashboards on the train before I even reach the office. I'm a junior campaign analyst at Northlight Media, a small agency of fourteen people, and I draft reports, test ad versions and clean up data, mostly with AI tools open all day. I did a marketing degree and passed, with no internships, and I live in a rented flat with my friend Joy. On weekends I write a newsletter for small-shop owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but then where's the revolution everyone promised? At the agency I'd keep using the tools anyway, because even small savings add up. Online I'd probably post a thread on which tools are genuinely useful and which are rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a little bored. I use AI every day to draft campaign reports and summarise ad data, and it's made me quicker than the other juniors. If it stalls, my edge shrinks, because everyone else catches up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job as a junior campaign analyst at Northlight Media, a small agency of fourteen people. I'd keep the newsletter I write on weekends about small-shop marketing, which brings in about 90 a month now. I'd put 200 a month into my loan, and ask for a raise at the one-year mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, mostly. I like my work, and money is okay though not roomy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the newsletter fit in, and who reads it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents run a bakery, and Dad says marketing is soft work. Mum is on my side. I'd tell them that a plateau is fine with me, because I'd rather build a real reputation than ride a bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge would shrink. How do you protect it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would I do if everyone had the same tools? I'd get better at the part AI can't do, like talking to clients and spotting what a brand really needs. Being quick won't be enough on its own, and I know it.

say: I'd say it's **fine**, but where's the revolution everyone promised?
I'd post online about which AI tools are **useful** and which are rubbish.
think: I'd be a little **bored**, because AI has made me quicker than the other juniors.
If everyone catches up, my **edge** shrinks.
do: Keep the weekend **newsletter**, which brings in about 90 a month.
Put **200 a month** into the loan.
Ask for a **raise** at the one-year mark.
feel: I feel **content**: I like my work and money is okay, if not roomy.
S0.quote: Being quick won't be enough on its own, and I know it.
fieldNote: Sara is a daily AI user, so a stalled world actually costs her a **head start**.
She is already running a small **side income**, which says a lot about her appetite for risk.

steps.text: Keep writing the weekend newsletter for small shops
Put 200 a month into the student loan
Ask Northlight for a raise at one year
Practise client calls to build skills AI can't copy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good and bad at once, and the only honest position is to learn it fast and demand fairness. At the agency I'd show the team how I use the tools. Online I'd argue that firms should share the gains with staff, because otherwise the owners keep all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is in the line of fire. Reporting, copy drafts, data checks and ad testing are all what the tools do. But I use them every day, so I might be the one who survives by running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Northlight to make me the AI lead for client reporting, with a pay rise to match. I'd grow the newsletter to a paid version, aiming for 300 a month by next year. I'd also keep 800 in a separate account in case my hours get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous, in about equal parts. I like being early, but I know that early doesn't mean safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show Magda the value of what you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency owner, Magda, is 58 and not a tech person. She'd probably cut two juniors if clients push on price. I'd make sure she sees me saving her time, with numbers, before she decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would going freelance look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost the job, I could live on savings for about two months. My parents would help with the rent in a pinch. I'd go freelance rather than wait for another agency to hire.

say: I'd tell people to learn the tools **fast** and demand that firms share the gains with staff.
I'd show colleagues how I **use** the tools.
think: My job is in the **line of fire**, since reports, drafts and data checks are what the tools do.
Using AI every day might make me the one who **survives**.
do: Ask Northlight to make me **AI lead** for client reporting, with a raise.
Grow the newsletter into a **paid version**, aiming for 300 a month.
Keep **800** in a separate account in case my hours are cut.
feel: I'm **excited** and nervous in equal parts, because early doesn't mean safe.
S1.quote: I like being early, but I know that early doesn't mean safe.
fieldNote: Sara sees herself as a likely **survivor** but knows her agency owner could still cut two juniors.
Her answer to risk is to make her work **visible** in numbers and to build a second income.

steps.text: Ask Northlight to make me AI lead for client reports
Turn the newsletter into a paid version
Hold 800 in a separate cushion account
Show owner Magda the hours I save with numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got two years to rewrite the rules, and that nobody is in charge of that yet. At work I'd push the agency to share its plan. Online I'd campaign for a tax on the companies making the gains, to pay for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think junior marketing analysis is done by 2028. If an AI can do my work better than me and cheaper, no agency keeps me for loyalty. I'm early on tools, but that only buys me a year, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I can, about 450 a month, and cut my lunches, trips and clothes. I'd turn the newsletter into the main thing and try to get ten corporate subscribers. I'd also look for work that depends on trust and hands, because those last three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and quite lucid about it. I'd have moments of panic, then I'd make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the move back to Ashby be like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd end up moving back near Mum and Dad above the bakery in Ashby, to cut rent. I'd help at the counter in the mornings if I had to. It isn't what I imagined at 22, but it's a floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be angry. Who is that anger for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also be angry at the people who told us to study business because it was safe. Nobody warned us that safe jobs depend on the speed of a company's software team. I'd say that to every person who would listen.

say: I'd say we have **two years** to rewrite the rules, and nobody is in charge of that.
I'd campaign online for a **tax** on the companies making the gains.
think: Junior marketing analysis is **done** by 2028, and being early on tools only buys me a year.
No agency keeps me out of **loyalty** if AI does my work better and cheaper.
do: Save about **450 a month** and cut lunches, trips and clothes.
Make the newsletter the **main thing** and aim for ten corporate subscribers.
Move back above the **bakery** in Ashby to cut rent.
feel: I'd be **frightened** but lucid, with moments of panic followed by lists.
S2.quote: Nobody warned us that safe jobs depend on the speed of a company's software team.
fieldNote: Sara believes her early AI use buys only a **short** head start before the agency can replace her.
Her anger points at advisers who called business degrees **safe**, and her fallback is family and the bakery.

steps.text: Save 450 a month and cut lunches and trips
Aim for ten corporate newsletter subscribers
Move back above the bakery in Ashby
Campaign online for a tax on AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something if we act now. At the agency I'd ask Magda for a long-term plan for the juniors. Online I'd say schools and governments need to start retraining people now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be okay if I keep moving. I have five years to become someone who can run things, not just do the tasks. The danger is waiting until year three to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in business analytics next autumn, 3,000 for the year. I'd take on a freelance client or two to build a name. I'd keep saving 250 a month, and I'd use my AI skills to teach local shops, maybe paid workshops on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, but not sick with it. Five years feels like a race I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your parents' bakery, and what would it teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd tell my parents is that the bakery should get an ordering system and online sales now. I could set it up for them. It would help them and give me real business experience at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to go all in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If year two shows the warning is real, I'd go all in on freelancing and workshops. If it looks slower, I'd stay at the agency for the salary and learning. I'd review it every six months with my friend Joy, who works in finance.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to build something if we act now.
I'd press schools and governments to start **retraining** now.
think: I'd be okay if I **keep moving** and become someone who runs things, not just does tasks.
The danger is waiting until **year three** to start.
do: Start a part-time **analytics course** next autumn, 3,000 for the year.
Take **freelance** clients and run paid Saturday workshops for local shops.
Save **250 a month** and set up online ordering at the bakery.
feel: I'd feel **alert** but not sick with it, like a race I can run.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a race I can run.
fieldNote: Sara treats five years as a **head start** and plans to turn her tool skills into teaching income.
She tests the plan on her family's **bakery** and reviews it every six months with a friend.

steps.text: Start a part-time business analytics course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and that people should use it to get an education that's about judgement. At work I'd carry on as usual. Online I'd say the real fight is over who gets the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'll be fine. By 32 I'd have a few careers' worth of experience, and a few years' head start on most people. I'd still want rules, because the people at the bottom don't get a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my analytics course, move into a strategy role at an agency or brand, and keep the newsletter as a second income. I'd save toward a small deposit, maybe 8,000 over four years. I'd also keep teaching workshops, because I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and curious about what I'd end up doing. A decade is a long time at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the real fight over gains look like for someone your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm wrong about being fine, I'd have time to change. That's the biggest difference for me. I wouldn't be fighting for scraps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by not fighting for scraps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd want is public investment in training and a shorter working week, so the gains don't just go up to owners. I'd vote on that and campaign for it. That feels like the thing that matters most.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and people should get an education about judgement.
I'd say the real fight is over who gets the **gains**.
think: I think I'll be **fine**, with a few careers' worth of experience by 32.
I'd still want rules, because people at the **bottom** don't get a head start.

Save about **8,000** over four years for a small deposit.
Keep the **workshops** and the newsletter as a second income.
feel: I feel **calm** and curious about what I'd end up doing.
S4.quote: I wouldn't be fighting for scraps.
fieldNote: Sara is **calm** because her adaptability and a decade give her room to change course.
She still pushes for **rules** and a shared share of the gains for people who can't adapt as fast.

steps.text: Finish the analytics course and aim for a strategy role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Two years is just enough to see my job go and not enough to build anything. What would help is public training money, a tax on the gains, and being able to show clients my own work, so I'm not just a junior who can be swapped.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe just that people think those of us who use the tools every day are fine. We're not fine, we're just early. Early is a head start, not a safe place.

headlineQuote: Early is a head start, not a safe place.
portrait: Sara is a marketing graduate, four months into a junior analyst job at a small agency, **renting** with a friend.
She uses AI every day and moves early, so a slow world bores her and a fast one frightens her.
Her mood climbs from calm to **alarmed** in the 2028 case, and her answer is always to build a second income.
She is progressive and wants **taxes** and public training, and her family bakery is her safety net.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most: two years is enough to lose her junior analyst job and too little to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Public **training** money, a tax on AI gains, and a body of her own work that clients can see.
